questions.stem: A motor has an input energy of 500 J and produces 350 J of useful kinetic energy. What is the efficiency of the motor?
questions.explanation: Efficiency = (useful output / total input) x 100 = (350 / 500) x 100 = 70%. Option A confuses useful and wasted energy (150 J wasted / 500 = 30% is the proportion wasted, not the efficiency). Option C gives units of joules, but efficiency is a ratio. Option D divides input by output, which gives a value over 100% and is impossible.

questions.stem: An electric heater is described as being nearly 100% efficient. Why is this possible for a heater but not for a light bulb?

options.text: Heaters use less electricity than light bulbs
The "wasted" thermal energy in a heater is actually the useful output
Heaters do not obey the law of conservation of energy
Light bulbs produce more energy than they consume

questions.explanation: For a heater, the purpose is to produce thermal energy, so virtually all input electrical energy becomes useful thermal output. For a light bulb, the useful output is light, and any thermal energy produced is wasted. All devices obey conservation of energy, and no device produces more energy than it consumes.

questions.stem: A power station burns fuel releasing 1000 MJ of energy and delivers 350 MJ of electrical energy. How much energy is wasted?
questions.explanation: Wasted energy = total input - useful output = 1000 - 350 = 650 MJ. The efficiency is 350/1000 = 35%, typical for a thermal power station. Most energy is wasted as heat in cooling towers and exhaust gases. Option B adds input and output, which has no physical meaning.

questions.stem: A machine has an efficiency of 0.80. If the useful power output is 2000 W, what is the total power input?
questions.explanation: Efficiency = useful output / total input, so total input = useful output / efficiency = 2000 / 0.80 = 2500 W. Option A multiplies output by efficiency instead of dividing (that would give the output from the input). Option C adds the wasted power incorrectly. The total input must always be greater than the useful output.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes would NOT improve the efficiency of a machine?

options.text: Lubricating moving parts to reduce friction
Using lighter materials to reduce weight

questions.explanation: Making a machine work faster increases its power output but does not change the proportion of useful energy to total energy (efficiency). Lubrication reduces friction losses, lighter materials reduce energy wasted moving the machine itself, and streamlining reduces air resistance losses. All of these reduce wasted energy and improve efficiency, but speed alone does not.
